Following the Crowd 
The State of UK Crowdfunding 
2020

Introduction
For many years, the chance to invest in promising private 
companies was exclusive to an elite few. Only those who 
actively managed funds, or who had substantial capital and 
industry links, could feasibly participate in funding, and 
eventually profit from the UK’s most exciting and 
high-growth companies. 
But this all changed with the advent of crowdfunding 
platforms, back in the 2000s. These organisations have 
eﬀectively democratised support for high-growth 
companies, and made it possible for novice and hobbyist 
investors to buy equity stakes in ambitious companies, from 
as little as £10. Thousands of investors can partake in a 
single round, each receiving a small equity stake in return, 
in the hope that the company will eventually undergo an 
IPO or an acquisition for a healthy sum.
This form of investing has come on leaps and bounds in the 
past decade. In 2011, only 8 deals were backed by 
crowdfunding websites; in 2019, crowdfunders backed 422 
deals, making them the second most active investor type, 
behind Venture Capital and Private Equity firms. 
But it’s not all about the money. Crowdfunding is a great way 
for businesses to engage an existing user base and reach new 
communities of people, building strong, lasting customer 
relationships.
In this report, we’ve explored the characteristics of these 
investments and how they’ve performed over time. We’ve 
also profiled the ten companies that have secured the largest 
amount of funding from the crowd in 2020 so far.

Definitions
Crowdfunded companies
Any UK company that has successfully raised finance 
through an equity crowdfunding platform since 2011. 
1,632 companies have secured crowdfunding between 
2011 and H1 2020. 
VC-backed / venture-backed companies
Any UK company that has successfully raised equity 
finance from a venture capital or private equity firm since 
2011 (unless otherwise stated), where we can confirm the 
identity of the investing fund. 
3,434 companies have secured venture funding between 
2011 and H1 2020. 
298 companies have secured both forms of funding, 
and are double counted in this analysis.

There are a wide range of diﬀerent investor types that can deploy equity funding 
in the UK, from angels and crowdfunders to VCs and government funds. But the 
characteristics of these funds, the manner in which they support company 
growth, and the profiles of recipient companies can vary drastically. 
The Lay of the Land

Most crowdfunding deals use a nominee structure to 
manage the investment on the crowd's behalf. So whilst 
other investor types, from VCs to angels, can be as involved 
or as hands oﬀ with their portfolio companies as they’d like, 
the crowd is precluded from this interaction.
Choosing to raise finance through crowdfunding allows 
founders to reduce the risk of taking on demanding new 
investors, allowing them to maintain greater control of the 
company’s direction.
But it also means forgoing the industry expertise, 
knowledge, and connections that funds and angel investors 
bring to the table. Indeed, many VCs will play an active role 
in their portfolio companies, often taking a seat on the 
board of directors and providing personalised guidance.
What makes crowdfunding 
diﬀerent?

Crowdfunded companies tend to be in earlier stages of 
evolution than VC-backed businesses. Historically, it’s been 
new B2C businesses that have pursued crowdfunding, 
sometimes with a new product or one that is still being 
developed. 
But these figures have been fluctuating over time. As 
crowdfunding has become a more popular and trusted form 
of investment, later-stage businesses are also turning to this 
collective form of finance. 
In 2013, 82% of crowdfunding deals were completed with 
seed stage companies. By the end of 2019 this figure had 
dropped to 49%.
Stages of Evolution
Stages of evolution of companies at deal date
2011 – H1 2020

Diﬀerences between investor types are also reflected in the 
exit and death rates of companies funded since 2011. 
Those that received capital from the crowd are almost twice 
as likely to have died, and four times less likely to have 
exited than VC-backed companies. 
Just 3% of crowdfunded companies have reached an IPO or 
successful acquisition, compared to 12% of venture-backed 
companies.
They are also less likely to have progressed to later stages of 
growth, instead stagnating in their current growth stages. 
Exit and Death Rates
Relative stage of evolution since time of fundraising
2011 – H1 2020

The geographic distribution of companies funded by 
crowdfunders versus venture capital and private equity 
funds is relatively similar. 
Both fund types invest heavily into London-based 
companies. Between 2011 and H1 2020, 873 companies in 
London have secured funding from the crowd, representing 
59% of all crowdfunded businesses in the UK.
In the same period, 1,679 London-based companies have 
secured funding from VC and PE firms, representing 58% of 
all venture-backed businesses in the UK. 
The next most popular destination for funding is the South 
East. 12% of crowdfunded businesses and 12% of 
venture-backed businesses are based in the South East. 
Geography  London

But there are some distinctions in the regional spread of 
companies backed by diﬀerent investor types. Crowdfunders 
are especially present in the South West, which is perhaps 
related to Crowdcube’s presence in Exeter. 
Venture funds tend to focus on the East of England, where there 
is a cluster of deeptech companies in and around Cambridge, as 
well as the North West and Scotland.

companies outside London

The State of the Market in 2020
Overall UK investment figures have declined over the past three halves, but 
how has crowdfunding fared? We’ve taken a closer look at the data to see how 
flows of investment have changed over time, and which platforms have 
facilitated the bulk of these transactions.

H2 2019 was the best half on record in terms of deal 
numbers, but H2 2018 saw the most pounds invested.
H1 2020 was the fourth highest half for the number of 
pounds invested by crowdfunders, but the third highest for 
number of deals completed.
Although crowdfunding activity decreased from H2 2019, 
both the number of deals and amount raised increased 
between H1 2019 and H1 2020. Against a tough backdrop, 
these figures are very positive.
But it’s unclear how, and to what extent, these figures will 
change in the near future. As the UK economy descends into 
a recession and the general public has less disposable 
income, we expect that crowdfunding activity will shrink 
further than that of institutional funds. 
Crowdfunding over time
Number of deals and amount raised via crowdfunding 
2017 – H1 2020

Crowdcube facilitated the most investment rounds of any 
UK platform in H1 2020, with 97 deals including 2 
pre-emption rounds.
Seedrs completed slightly fewer deals, but at a higher 
average ticket price, with a total of £49.7m invested over 95 
deals, including 27 pre-emption rounds.
A pre-emption round oﬀers existing investors the chance to 
buy new shares from a business, before new investors. This 
allows existing investors to maintain their stake in the 
company and avoid dilution. Only existing investors can 
invest in these rounds.
Top platforms H1 2020
Number of deals and amount raised per platform
H1 2020

The Impact of Coronavirus
The coronavirus outbreak has had a massive eﬀect on businesses across the 
globe. But not all businesses have been impacted equally. Our research shows 
that crowdfunded companies are more likely to be negatively impacted by 
COVID-19 than companies that have received VC backing.

The Impact of COVID-19
Impact of COVID-19 on crowdfunded companies
The increase in the proportion of positively impacted 
businesses between the beginning of May and the beginning 
of June suggests that VC-backed businesses were quicker to 
adapt their business operations.
Whilst there’s been a decrease in the severity of business 
impact across both crowdfunded and VC-backed 
companies, those that have the backing of a venture capital 
fund are more likely to have bounced back. Currently, 17% 
of crowdfunded companies have experienced a positive 
impact, compared to 26% of VC-backed businesses. 
Impact of COVID-19 on VC-backed companies

Crowdfunded companies are more likely to cater to 
consumers, whereas VC-backed companies are more likely 
to cater to businesses and the public sector. 
Factors at play  Target markets
With so much of normal life on hold, and less consumer 
spending, it’s not surprising that crowdfunded companies 
have been more negatively impacted. 
Crowdfunded companies
H1 2020
VC-backed companies
H1 2020

VC-backed companies are more likely to be in remote-ready 
sectors, such as internet platforms, business banking and 
security. 
Factors at play   Sectors
On top of this, crowdfunded companies are more likely to 
be in highly-impacted sectors, such as food & drinks and 
clothing, which took a much harder hit during lockdown.

Top 10 crowdfunded companies 2020
We’ve profiled the ten companies that have raised the most money through 
crowdfunding in H1 2020. Unsurprisingly, there are a number of fintechs on the 
list, but there are also some unlikely features. From vegan subscription boxes to 
sustainable toilet roll, these are the crowd’s top picks.

The most recent of these rounds took place in May, and 
totalled £6.69m. The round was completed in just five days 
with participation from 8,500 investors.
This capital will be used to grow Freetrade’s headcount and 
further expand its customer base in the UK and Europe. It 
will soon be launching Freetrade Plus, a premium account.
1.   Freetrade | £6.69m
Founded  2015
Sector  Fintech
Location  Tower Hamlets
Freetrade is developing a commission fee-free platform for 
investing in stocks and funds. Founded in 2015, and already 
used by over 200,000 customers, its mission is to make the 
process of investing more accessible, simple and cheaper. 
To date, the growth stage company has raised £24.5m over 
seven funding rounds. Six of these rounds included 
participation from the crowd, all facilitated by Crowdcube

£21m in funding and is currently in the venture stage of 
evolution. 
In January 2020, B-North raised more than £3.7m in funding 
through two separate crowdfunding platforms, Crowdcube 
(£2m) and Growthfunders (£1.7m). This was followed by an 
additional round through Growthfunders in April, which 
totalled £2.04m. Combined, these rounds are worth nearly 
£6m. The money raised will allow B-North to continue 
expanding its workforce and infrastructure. 
2.   B-North | £5.74m
Founded  2017
Sector  Fintech
Location  Manchester
B-North operates a bank, focussing on SME lending, with the 
aim to lend up to ten times faster than incumbent banks. 
The company plans to use a combination of fintech and 
face-to-face services through pop up lending pods. Once 
operational, the bank will deliver loans of between £500k 
and £5m to ambitious small businesses looking to scale up.
To date, the Manchester-based startup has raised a total of

The company completed its first crowdfunding campaign in 
March 2020 through Seedrs. The initial funding goal was 
£2m, but this was quickly met after 48 hours. It then went on 
to raise a total of £4.01m and welcomed a total of 1,800 
investors on board. 
The funds from this round are being used to build a bigger 
kitchen, develop new food categories and increase the 
weekly production of meals to over 60,000.
3.   Allplants | £4.01m
Founded  2016
Sector  Food & Drink
Location  Haringey
London startup Allplants provides a subscription box of 
vegan meals. Brothers Alex and Jonathan Petrides started 
the company in 2016 to make it easier for people to 
incorporate plant-based meals into their diets. 
Allplants has recently celebrated serving one million vegan 
meals from its kitchen in North London, and has received 
several Great Taste Gold Star Awards. To date, it has secured 
a total of £13.8m in equity fundraising and is currently in the 
venture stage of evolution.

In March 2020 Bidvine raised £2.76m in equity crowdfunding 
through Seedrs. Funds from the round will be used to 
continue to develop the UK marketplace, expanding into 
international markets and the introduction of additional 
tools for service professionals. 
To date, the company has secured a total of £9.18m in 
equity fundraisings. By 2025, Bidvine plans to have helped 
250,000 local businesses and added 200,000 jobs to its 
platform.
4.   Bidvine | £2.76m
Founded  2014
Sector  Services on Demand
Location  City of London
Bidvine has developed an online service that puts 
customers in touch with local service providers such as 
tutors, fitness instructors and photographers. For service 
providers, the platform oﬀers a cost per lead marketing 
option designed to bring new customers to their business. 
Bidvine first launched in 2014 and is now in the venture 
stage of evolution, with over 300 services on oﬀer and more 
than 100,000 registered professionals.

The funding will be used to kit out Innis & Gunn’s interior 
brewhouse, improve warehousing capability, and visitor 
experience. 
It will also go towards building Edinburgh's largest brewery 
in 150 years at Heriot-Watt University’s Research Park. As a 
small token of gratitude, each Innis & Gunn investor will 
have their name displayed on the wall of the brewery.
5.   Innis & Gunn | £2.63m
Founded  2003
Sector  Food & Drink
Location  Edinburgh
Brewery Innis & Gunn operates multiple bars and produces 
a range of craft beers. Since 2003, the company has been 
brewing up a wide range of flavoured beers which they sell 
in over 35 countries. In 2019 the company won the New York 
International Beer Awards and Scottish Brewery of the Year.
Innis & Gunn raised £2.63m of funding in February 2020 
through a successful crowdfunding campaign with Seedrs. 
Over 3,000 investors participated, with investment coming 
from across the UK and Europe.

The most recent round was raised in April 2020 and totalled 
£2.57m. Over 4,000 backers took part and the initial £1m 
target was reached in just a few hours. 
The following month it was revealed that Chip had scored 
FCA authorisation as an Authorised Payments Institution for 
its money-saving app. The funds from the latest 
crowdfunding round will be used to launch a new type of 
savings account and to continue supporting their growth. 
6.   Chip | £2.57m
Founded  2016
Sector   Fintech
Location  City of London
Chip develops a savings account app that connects to users’ 
current bank account and uses artificial intelligence to 
determine how much they can aﬀord to save, putting this 
away automatically. 
Founded in 2016, it has already raised a total of £14.8m in 
equity investment, with much of this secured through 
crowdfunding. The AI-powered savings app has gained over 
11,000 shareholders from four fundraising campaigns on the 
Crowdcube platform.

The venture stage company first took to equity 
crowdfunding back in 2016, when it launched a successful 
rewards-based campaign. Cheeky Panda’s most recent and 
largest raise was in May 2020, when it secured £2.41m 
through Seedrs, despite an initial target of just £750k. 
The company also raised £1m in equity fundraising in July 
2018 from VC firm Northern & Shell Ventures. This takes 
Cheeky Panda’s total fundraisings to date to £5.83m.
7.   The Cheeky Panda | £2.41m
Founded  2016
Sector  Household Goods
Location  City of London
The Cheeky Panda produces sustainable toilet paper from 
waste bamboo, aiming to reduce deforestation and 
chemical use in the manufacturing process. The startup 
launched in 2016, with the mission to encourage consumers 
to switch to more sustainable products. 
The Cheeky Panda has expanded to over 20 international 
markets and listed with major retailers, including the likes of 
WHSmith, Boots and Amazon.

In May of this year, TV.FIT raised £2.2m in crowdfunding 
through Seedrs, attracting 300 investors. This was the 
company's first crowdfunding campaign and was launched 
in April with an initial funding target of £1.4m, which was 
quickly surpassed. 
Funds will be used to grow and expand the TV.FIT platform 
and possibly contribute to the repayment of some debt. 
This takes TV.FIT’s total fundraisings to £3.97m. 
8.   TV.FIT | £2.20m
Founded  2016
Sector  Health & Fitness
Location  East Dunbartonshire
TV.FIT provides tailored home and online workout classes 
with fitness experts and celebrities. The company’s at-home 
health solution is designed for all ages and levels, allowing 
people to work out in the flexibility and comfort of their own 
homes in exchange for a monthly subscription. 
Launched in 2016, TV.FIT is currently in the seed stage and 
based in the West of Scotland, with subscribers in 66 
countries across the world.

Cushon is no stranger to crowdfunding, having completed 
several successful campaigns since 2018. Most recently, in 
May 2020, it raised £2.17m through Seedrs, which has taken 
their total amount raised through crowdfunding to £6.38m. 
This most recent round was part of a wider £7m fundraising 
led by family oﬀice Major Oak. Cushon has already used 
some of this investment for its recent acquisition of Salvus, 
and is now using the remaining balance to focus on market 
growth and product development.
9.   Cushon | £2.17m
Founded  2017
Sector  Fintech
Location  Dorset
Cushon (formerly Smarterly) operates an online platform 
that oﬀers workplace savings schemes. It lists a number of 
investment funds and ISAs designed to help simplify the 
investment process. The company rebrand comes shortly 
after it entered the pensions market through its acquisition 
of Salvus Master Trust. 
Since being founded in 2017, the fintech has gone on to 
work with over 100 large businesses and now has over 
80,000 customers, with £250m assets under management. 
To date, it has secured a total of £11.9m in fundraisings.

In June 2020, ABM Communications raised £2.14m in its first 
crowdfunding raise. This has taken their total fundraisings 
secured to £8.14m.
The initial funding is being used to drive distribution deals 
through content and marketing. By 2024, ABM 
Communications hopes to have grown its subscriber base to 
over 800,000 and have widened its distribution footprint. 
10.   ABM Comms | £2.14m
Founded  2017
Sector  Media Production
Location  Camden
ABM Communications oﬀers on-demand, 
subscription-based television streaming services designed 
to provide content that gives the back story for audiences. 
Its first channel, True Royalty, is dedicated to featuring royal 
dramas and documentaries. This channel is available in the 
USA, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, Ireland, and the UK, 
with plans to expand into other regions soon. 
Founded in 2017, the London-based media production 
company is already in the venture stage of growth and has 
achieved significant popularity, particularly in America.
